newsitem.title: USA: U.S. urges Zaire's neighbors to keep out of war.
newsitem.headline: U.S. urges Zaire's neighbors to keep out of war.

text.p: The United States said on Wednesday it had urged Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi to stay out of fighting in eastern Zaire between Tutsi-led rebels and Zairean government forces.

"The United States appeals again to the neighbours of Zaire to stay out of Zaire, to not involve themselves in the fighting," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said. "We have underscored this message to Uganda and Rwanda and Burundi."

The rebels launched their revolt in October, accusing Zaire of denying them citizenship and seeking to return them to Rwanda, which their forebears left generations ago. An army counter-offensive has made little apparent headway.
"We're concerned about this situation and Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright has taken the opportunity over the last 24 hours to transmit this message," Burns told a news briefing.
He said Albright had raised the issue at Washington meetings on Tuesday with Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and on Wednesday with Belgian Foreign Minister Erick Derycke.
Burns did not directly accuse Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of intervening in Zaire, but U.S. officials said there had been allegations of this.
The United States urged previously that there should be no foreign intervention in the Zaire conflict, but this was the first time Burns named the three countries.

A senior U.S. official said: "President Museveni's position yesterday was that, well, there were just some border clashes because actually there were insurgents on the Zairean part of the border attacking Uganda and therefore Uganda had to respond -- it's kind of a hot pursuit issue."

"Secretary Albright just made the point that we think this is fundamentally destabilising at a time when Zaire has become a quite unstable place," said the official, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Burns said one of Washington's concerns was that 200,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees, who fled their own country in a 1994 civil war, remained trapped in eastern Zaire by the fighting.
He said he believed the United States shared a common position on the issue with France and Belgium, both former colonial powers in the region.
"We do believe that the French, the Belgians and the Americans together can have influence on those neighbouring governments," he said.

"In the case of Rwanda -- we've done quite a lot for Rwanda, and we've had good relations with Uganda as well, and with Burundi. We've done quite a lot for these countries on a humanitarian basis and we think they ought to tend to their own problems at home."
A Belgian diplomatic source said one of Derycke's aims in Washington was to "ring the alarm bells over Central Africa and stress that Belgium cannot solve this problem alone".
He said the United States, France and Belgium, traditional allies in dealing with Central Africa, needed to form a united front to approach the crisis.

The source said Belgium would like the United States and France to help accomplish two goals -- to hold democratic elections in Zaire and to stage a Central African conference with other African countries to map out a future for the region.
